title: Review: Energy levels and spectra; Potential difference and emf; Wave–particle duality
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: Q02-uk1#t2 term and clue written for the game; Q02-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; Q02-uk1#t1 term and clue written for the game; Q03-1#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL02-1#N.13b, Q02-1#N.6a, Q02-uk1#N.10, Q03-1#N.17b, EL02-1#N.3a, Q02-1#N.13a, Q02-uk1#N.3, Q03-1#N.4a. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Continuous spectrum
items.clue: Light containing all wavelengths, given out by a star's hot, dense surface.

items.label: Absorption line spectrum
items.clue: Dark gaps at fixed wavelengths, seen when white light has passed through a cooler gas.

items.label: Discharge tube
items.clue: Low-pressure gas with a high p.d. across it, used to make a gas emit its bright lines.

items.label: Electron diffraction
items.clue: Bright concentric rings on a fluorescent screen after a beam passes through thin graphite.

questions.stem: While a kettle is heating water, 2.0 × 10³ C of charge passes through its heating element and 4.6 × 10⁵ J of energy is transferred in the element. What is the potential difference across the element?
An atom has only four energy levels: −1.50 eV, −2.50 eV, −4.00 eV and −6.00 eV. What is the energy of the emitted photon that has the SHORTEST wavelength?
questions.explanation: Largest gap: −1.50 eV → −6.00 eV, ΔE = 4.50 eV. Largest ΔE → highest f → shortest λ.

questions.stem: A cool cloud of gas lies in front of a hot star, and the star's spectrum seen through the cloud has dark lines. A second telescope views the same cloud from the side, against dark sky, with no star behind it. What does the second telescope see?

options.text: The same dark lines on a continuous band.
A continuous band with no lines.
Nothing at all: the gas absorbs light but does not emit it.
Bright lines at the same wavelengths as the dark lines.

questions.explanation: The atoms re-emit the absorbed photons in all directions. From the side, only those wavelengths arrive: bright lines on a dark background, at the dark lines' wavelengths.

questions.stem: A beam of electrons and a beam of protons are each accelerated from rest through 100 V and aimed at the same crystal, whose rows of atoms are 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m apart. Which beam shows clear diffraction?

options.text: Only the protons: they are heavier, so they hit the atoms harder and are scattered more.
Both equally: they have the same charge and the same p.d., so they gain the same energy.
Only the electrons: their wavelength is comparable with the spacing of the atoms.
Neither: diffraction is a property of waves, and both beams are made of particles.

questions.stem: A steady current of 0.50 A flows through a small electric motor for 2.0 minutes. In this time, 360 J of energy is transferred from electrical energy to other forms in the motor. What is the potential difference across the motor?
An atom has energy levels at −10.0 eV (the ground state), −5.0 eV and −3.0 eV. An atom in its ground state is struck by a photon of energy 3.0 eV. What happens?

options.text: The photon is absorbed, and the electron moves up to the −3.0 eV energy level.
The photon is not absorbed, as it matches neither gap from the ground state, 15.0 or 13.0 eV.
The photon is not absorbed, as it matches neither gap from the ground state, 5.0 or 7.0 eV.
The photon is absorbed, and the electron moves up to an energy of −7.0 eV.

questions.stem: Hydrogen atoms in the ground state are bombarded by electrons, each with kinetic energy 12.5 eV. The lowest levels of hydrogen are −13.6 eV, −3.40 eV, −1.51 eV and −0.85 eV. Which can happen in a single collision?

options.text: Nothing, as 12.5 eV does not exactly match any gap from the ground state.
The atom is excited to n = 4, as the electron gives up all of its 12.5 eV.
The atom is ionised, and the electron moves on with 1.1 eV.
The atom is excited to n = 3, and the electron moves on with 0.4 eV.

questions.explanation: The n = 1 → n = 3 gap is 13.6 − 1.51 = 12.09 eV. The electron gives 12.09 eV and keeps 12.5 − 12.09 ≈ 0.4 eV. (Excitation to n = 2 is also possible.)

questions.stem: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 2.0 kV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and treat the electron as non-relativistic. What is the de Broglie wavelength of the electron?
